Text.Text: Symphonies, the highest discipline of composing, usually consisting of four movements.
Pieces written for the big stage, singers with main character syndrome and a huge orchestra.
Works that are written after a story, primarily for an Orchestra.
Cycles, Pieces and a Concerto for Solo Piano.
A collection of Waltzes and other folkloristic pieces
Pieces written for the classical guitar.
Build next to a Bauxite, Mineral, Iron or Gold Ore Mine to mine for extra Silver Ore.

Composer Pyotr Tchaikovsky writes of death and transience. This symphony almost sounds like a requiem to himself, especially in the fourth movement. It seems to follow some program, although he did not want to tell anyone about it, stating that it shall remain a mystery to everyone. The subtitle “Pathétique” is linked to a piano sonata by Beethoven with the same name, but was assigned retroactively on idea of his brother Modest.

A falling-second motif, almost a wailing cry, is woven through to the entire work. The second movement is entirely in 5/4-meter, something unusual for the waltz-like or minuet character this movement evokes, it rather is more prominent in Russian folk music.

After the third movement, where a march theme is becoming more and more important, people always tend to clap, probably for its finalistic character. It is important not to do so, as a fourth movement is following, which does not end as a triumphant Finale, instead slowly fading into darkness and silence. It becomes apparent that the symphony's hidden program probably includes death, but Tchaikovsky will take that information to his grave.
Antonín Dvořák: Symphony No. 9 "Z nového světa"

World-renowned composer Antonin Dvorak has, after a recent stay in Vespuccia, which he refers to as the “New World”, composed another symphony, and it shall become known as his best. In it, the composer processes a multitude of impressions, such as the sheer size of the American cities, where skyscrapers as high as the Skyline Tower are a common sight.

In the tradition of “national music”, in which composers try to find the musical language of a nation's culture, Dvorak tries to write a distinctly American piece. “There is Italian, German, French, Czech and Russian Music, why shouldn’t there be an American one?” he said.

For his characterization of “American” music, he draws from two influences: First, Afro-American spiritual, which his assistant Harry Thacker Burleigh, later referred to as “father of the spiritual” sang to him. Secondly, he refers to music of the Native Americans, who have become a more and more rare sight in the past years. As such, Dvorak visited shows of world-renowned showman Buffalo Bill to get an impression of it.

The influence of John Longfellows poem Hiawatha becomes apparent in the second and third movement, the former being a sketch for a future composition Dvorak hinted at writing only recently, and the latter movement Scherzo being inspired by the celebration scene.

An impressionist piece through and through, the title Estampes refers to the technique of engraving artwork into materials like wood. The three movements are mostly disjointed, but form a trilogy that describes impressions from different parts of the world.

Pagodes is written about the Pagodas of Horai, namely the Java region of it, and in the same way that the Pagodas are the same floor and roof stacked multiple times, part of the motif of Pagodes climbs up through three octaves, while the entire motif describes the shape of a single Pagoda roof. The piece references Javanese Gamelan music with pentatonic scales and the left hand emulating its structural drum.

La Soirée dans Grenade is about the Andalusia region in Spain. The piece has multiple themes, a theme with mauric influences and two habaneras in the style of a dance from the Spanish Cuba province, joined by a motif that emulates moving a single chord upwards on a guitar fretboard, and one inspired by the castagnette, a national instrument of Spain. Debussy had never been to either Java nor Andalusia, with these impressions instead originating from the famous Paris World’s Fair.

Jardins sous la pluie is about children playing in a garden in Paris while it is raining. The rain is represented by fast 16th and 8th notes, the children through the quotation of two French children's songs, Do, do, l'enfant do and Nous n'irons plus au bois.

British composer Edward Elgar wrote 14 character pieces in a cycle of variations over a common theme which he invented himself. The work is, as the name says, an enigma, being dedicated “to my friends pictured within” by Elgar, although the title Enigma originates from a friend, only being adopted by him.

The movements bear nicknames of his friends, with C.A.E for his wife Caroline Alice Elgar, or E.D.U. as his three-letter pet name being the first and last movement. For each movement, Elgar pictures “the way in which this specific friend would have written the variation - would they be dumb enaugh to compose”.

Yet another Waltz from the Strauss family in the so typically viennese 3/4-rhythm, with the second beat moved forwards a little… This waltz is about the times of spring, with bird voices evoked through happy flute motives.

This piece exists in two versions, one with voice as a coloratura waltz, one without as a concert waltz version, with the instrumentation changing between the voice and orchestral version. The optional text by Richard Genée transliterates the meaning of the music into words:

Die Lerche in blaue Höh entschwebt,
der Tauwind weht so lau;
sein wonniger milder Hauch belebt
und küßt das Feld, die Au.

The lark levitates away into the blue sky,
the thaw wind blows so lukewarm,
his blissful mild breath enlives
and kisses the field, the meadow

Another piano cycle on the program, Spanish composer Albeniz writes characteristic pieces about regions in La Corona’s empire, paying homage to the rich history of the Spanish provinces and cities, a Serenade for Granada, a Courante for Catalonia, a Fantasy for Aragón, and a Nocturne for the then-province of Cuba.

Further, the suite pays homage to the former kingdom of Asturias in form that Albeniz calls “Leyenda”, meaning “legend”. The piece starts and ends with a persistent bassline continuing for minutes on end, only varying in accompaniment, only interrupted by a brief and flimmering episode of calmness that reminds of the burning heat of the Spanish streets. For Sevilla, Albeniz writes in the style of an Andalusian flamenco folk dance, the Sevillianas, picking up on its primary rhythm, but disregarding the traditional chord structure. The city of Cadíz is represented through a stylized Saeta in the middle part of the piece, a religious and pious singing style native to Spain, sung primarily for the holy week before Easter. This suite is completed by “Castilla”, written in a Seguidilla structure.

The trumpet solo right at the start of the symphony calls the audience to a funeral march, and sends any trumpet player who fumbles it on stage straight to hell. This fanfare is restated numerous times throughout the movement, joined by a longing melody of sorrow, and a more passionate passage, with the latter character being picked up on in the second movement.

Mahler breaks with the usual symphonic four-movement structure (Kopfsatz - Slow - Scherzo or Minuet - Finale ), giving this symphony five movements instead of the usual four, swapping the first two movements and introducing an “Adagietto” as the fourth movement before the Finale. In this five movement structure, the first two and last two form a unit, which comparts the work into three parts.

After the funeral march in the first movement, the deep-dive into hell of the second, and the powerful and energetic third movement, which Mahler himself describes as “sounds from a primeval world”, “dancing stars” and “shimmering, glittering waves” , the fourth movement speaks of love, or more precisely of how one imagines and wants love to be - because with Mahler, everything has a double meaning: “Could love only be like this Adagietto makes it sound”. The symphony ends with happiness and joy in a sparkling Finale.

This piece takes a short time to learn, but a long time to play. Satie only wrote two lines of music for this piece, but advises the performer to play them 840 times. Through this, he puts the performer through a form of mental and physical torment and torture.

Neither of the two lines is understandable, not the first one, written as a single “melody” - which really is more a sequence of notes, nor the more chordal one, that adds other tone rows underneath the first one. This complete non-melody probably is exactly what Satie intended. Through the simple act of repetition, a short search for any sort of melody or structure becomes a never-ending one that always tends to look in the same spots, but can never find anything. Although, interestingly the piece shares structural tone material with “Bonjour, Biqui, Bonjour”, written by Satie for his then-crush.

Few performers are able to finish this piece in its completeness, with common performance methods being multiple performers or reducing the amount of repetitions.

The unusual and unconventional name of this piano cycle by German composer Robert Schumann alludes to the fictitious figure of chapel master Kreisler, who originates from the writings of E.T.A. Hoffmann and appears in works as the “Kreisleriana” texts, “der goldene Topf” and “Lebensansichten des Katers Murr”. The fictitious figure of Kreisler is based on composer Ludwig Böhner, who Schumann met years before writing this piece.

In Hoffmann's work, pianist Kreisler has to play from Johann Sebastian Bach's Goldberg Variations, which Schumann puts into music by ripping some figures directly from the Bach piece and weaving them into his composition, Schumann's intermezzo directly relates to the 17th variation, and there are distant allusions to Bach's “the art of the fugue” and “well-tempered clavier” in the other movements.

The piece leads towards the extreme, oversketching aspects of Kreisler's character, painting a picture of a torn and extravagant individual. In this manner, the Kreisleriana is a deeply psychological work, with a lot of meta-connections built to Hoffman's writings. Apart from numerous character aspects, Kreisler's eventual disappearance is alluded to in the eighth and final movement.

Two versions exist of the Hungarian dance: one for four-handed piano, and an arrangement for Orchestra, and in case of the first Hungarian dance, both versions are written by Brahms himself.
Adapting “Hungarian” music is very popular in the work of German and Austro-Hungarian composers, such as Roma folk music forms like the Czardas and Verbunkos into their work. Johannes Brahms, in his Hungarian dance does not use original Roma tunes, but they are arrangements of dances and themes he learned from violinist Eduard Reményi, some of them composed by that violinist.
The fifth Hungarian dance in particular is based on a theme by Hungarian composer Béla Kéler, who wrote it for his work “Erinnerung an Bartfeld”. Thus, most of the pieces are not Brahms' own work, he simply arranged them.

Written for a small ensemble of strings, “Transfigured Night” by Jewish-Austrian composer Arnold Schönberg is a programmatic work about a poem of Richard Dehmel. On a walk in a cold moon night, a woman reveals to the man that she loves that she is pregnant, though the child is not his, but of the man she married once - not for love, but to become a mother.

Schönberg's piece describes different feelings throughout the poem, focusing much more on emotions than on the plot: The cold moon night, the woman's revelation, her unhappiness and loneliness, her forced loyalty for her husband, each get their own movement.

A duet between cello and violin musically describes the man forgiving his beloved and telling her that she will bear the child as if it was his, only to end in a new theme of the warmth of love.
Maurice Ravel: Valses nobles et sentimentales

French composer Maurice Ravel writes a cycle of seven Waltzes, each one bending the form of the waltz to its limit. Following the idea of Franz Schubert’s collections of Valses nobles and valses sentimentales, Ravel writes a modern version of them in his own style, which especially in terms of harmony is different from Schubert's, leading seamlessly into the next century instead of alluding to the past one.

All seven movements are sentimental or noble, although some are more noble than sentimental - the differentiation is not as clear as in Schubert’s cycles. The first movement is very noble, a parade-like introduction to the work, with the fourth movement “Asset animé” particularly picking up on a more avant-garde definition of nobility, featuring harmonic changes that are highly unusual and held together through creativity and exploitation of symmetric chord structures.

The second waltz in particular is sentimental, whereas start and end are a search in very undefined spaces, the central part offers prettier and more understandable passages, thus piecing the sound together and then disbanding it again. The seventh movement is a homage to Johann Strauß, the king of viennese waltzes, before the cycle ends with an epilogue that combines and summarizes the different movements.

Recognizable from the first two notes alone, Polish composer Fryderyk Chopin’s Nocturne in e-flat major is a piece that radiates cuteness and dreamyness over anything else. The piece is quite short, and thus uses very simplistic elements, stating the initial phrase once, then repeating a decorated version of it. Then follows a second phrase, which develops into something more melancholic and sentimental, before going back to the initial phrase in even more decorated versions.

Through the repeated usage of decoration, deepening and extending the sweet character of the melody, seemingly like putting a compliment into even warmer words every time, Chopin builds states the same idea in various degrees of embellishment, cementing it as the central idea to the piece.

The piece ends with an elongated tail section that picks up on the melancholic character of the second idea, through the use of the minor four chord in a major key, that gradually transforms back into the central melody of the first phrase.
Modest Mussorgsky: Pictures of an Exhibition

A memorial exhibition of German-Russian painter Viktor Hartmann is set to music by Modest Mussorgsky. Each of the movements is about a painting in the exhibition, with the connecting element in form of a short movement called “Promenade” appearing in different instrumentations, which directly translates moving from one painting to the next.

The character pieces come with big variety, putting “Gnomus”, a piece on a small gnome and about his styles of movement - fast movements, sudden standstill and sinister sneaking, next to “Tuileries”, which contrasts the playful and happy children with the admonishing educators wish for restraint in the famous Parisian park, and Bydło, a picture about an oxen cart passing by on a road in Poland, and also a grotesque movement about chicks in eggshells, where the music paints their vivid nature.

Following, there is a movement on the Russian story of Baba Yaga, a witch in a dark forest who tries to eat passerbys. The devilish call of the Witch is marked by a tritone and the pounding rhythm marks the mortar tool she uses to fly. The last picture in the exhibition is the great gate of Kyiv, for which Hartmann made a draft, with the music building a majestic character with a lot of ornamentation in form of scales, which symbolically refer to the architectural ornaments in the draft.
Sergei Rachmaninoff: Isle of the Dead

After seeing a black-and-white copy of the identically named painting by Arnold Böcklin, Rachmaninov composed a symphonic poem on it, recently stating that, had he seen the colorful original, the composition would have sounded a bit different.
The painting features a small rowboat to the central isle of the dead, which in Rachmaninov's piece is marked in the rhythm: an unusual 5-meter represents the somewhat irregular movement of rowing and of the waves of the sea. Through the long buildup of instrumentation from low notes to full orchestra, the island seems to slowly appear from the mist, and also slowly lets it disappear into the mist in the third part of the piece.
Through a melody that is hundreds of years old, the infamous plainchant motif “Dies Irae”, Rachmaninov represents death, and this four-note melody is woven in over and over again, especially in the middle of the piece, which focuses more on the island than on the sea around it.

Programmatic music, aka music that attempts to render an idea outside of music, is especially common in the Romantic period. British composer Gustav Holst picks the planets of the solar system as the program for this suite, but mainly referring to their astrological properties, that are also close to the characters the planets are named after, roman gods that already were worshipped in the temples of Latium.

The suite starts with Mars, the bringer of War, with the music describing his brute force and destructive power with strong brass and an unsettling, persistent 5-beat rhythm. Venus, bringer of peace, is a very calm and tranquil piece. Mercury, the winged messenger, features rapid changes in rhythm and uneven meters, representing his speedy flight. The movement for Jupiter depicts the joy and optimism through solemn fanfares, with the central melody also being used by Holst in the patriotic hymn “I vow to thee, my country”.

While Saturn gets a grave and heavy movement, representing maturity and age, Uranus, the magician, is a much more energetic movement of unexpectancy. The piece ends with Neptune, the mystical, a planet only discovered this century - now we finally have them all! - his mystical properties are built into sphaeric sounds, featuring revolutionary fade-out technique, accomplished by closing the door of the choir room to the stage.

“Bruckner is half genius, half fool”, conductor Hans von Bülow said about Austrian composer Anton Bruckner, and he might be right: Between the beautiful melodies and passages extending to epic proportions, Bruckner also is a master of repeating things, especially the introduction of his symphonies.

Bruckner’s Symphony, referred to as “the romantic one” reaches monumental extents, featuring an additional horn theme on top of the usual two themes in a symphony. Bruckner gave some hints on how to play the first movement, but they should not be confused with an actual program - they are more an allegory than anything else: “Medieval town - dawn - wake-up calls from the city towers - gates open… - forest, birds chirping” - and thus, the secondary theme evokes the singing of a titmouse.

The scherzo is in a very unusual 2-meter instead of the usual 3-meter, but still keeping the uplifting spirit of the form, and it is full of powerful horn passages. The Finale is a full-circle moment back to the first movement, with a lot of similar passages and backreference, building up to a grand and dramatic Coda at the end, which has almost cinematic character, constructed from the initial horn theme.
Camille Saint-Saëns: Le Carnaval des animaux

This work by the French composer with the unpronounceable surname is a parade of parody, depicting the character of a lot of animals in a humorous fashion. The piece, written for chamber orchestra parodizes a multitude of popular songs and works of other French composers.

The introduction leads directly to the apex animal: The Lion, king of the animals, gets a royal march, in which his roar is imitated by fast scale runs of pianos and strings. The turtles dance Jaques Offenbach’s famous "Can-Can" in slow motion, while for the elephant, Mendelssohn’s light-footed "Sommernachtstraum" scherzo plays on the heavy double bass. Jumpy rhythms for kangaroos on the piano, the Aquarium with rising bubbles turned into sound by a glass harmonica, violins playing a literal donkey noise for “Personalities with long Ears”, and a piece where instruments imitate the chirping of different birds.

The 12th movement, Fossiles, is full of quotations of popular songs: "Au clair de la lune", "partant pour la Syrie", "ah! vous dirai-je maman", "J’ai du bon tabac", as well as quotations from the composers “Danse Macabre” and "Una voce poco" by Rossini. All of the quotations are pieces of older times, musical “fossils”,that are often played on a Xylophone for its dry sound.

The last movement, the swan, is radiating elegance and beauty, and is one of the few movements that is not a parody, before the finale is a summary where each animal shows up very shortly again.

Thaïs by French composer Jules Massenet, is set in Roman-ruled Egypt and centers on Athanaël, a severe Christian monk who becomes obsessed with saving Thaïs, a famous courtesan in Alexandria. Believing her beauty and sensual life are corrupting the city, he goes to confront her and persuade her to abandon pleasure for religion.Thaïs first mocks him, but she is shaken by his certainty and by her own fear of aging, death, and spiritual emptiness. It is at this point that a transitory piece called Meditation is played between pictures, that marks the transition of Thaïs from courtesan to saint.

Athanaël eventually convinces Thaïs to renounce her old life. She burns her possessions and follows him across the desert to a convent, where she is received by the nuns and begins a life of penitence. But as Thaïs becomes more spiritually pure, Athanaël discovers that his own motives were not pure at all: he is tormented by desire for her and realizes he has confused religious zeal with repressed passion.

In the final scene, Thaïs lies dying in the convent, filled with visions of heavenly peace. Athanaël rushes to her and confesses that he loves her, begging her to live and return his love. Thaïs, however, no longer belongs to the earthly world and dies in religious ecstasy. Athanaël is left broken, spiritually defeated by the very salvation he thought he had brought her.

La Traviata follows Violetta Valéry, a celebrated Parisian courtesan who lives for pleasure despite suffering from tuberculosis. At a party, she meets Alfredo Germont, a sincere young man who has loved her from afar. His devotion moves her, and although she initially resists the idea of real love, she eventually leaves her glamorous social world to live with him in the countryside.

Their happiness is interrupted by Alfredo’s father, Giorgio Germont, who visits Violetta and begs her to end the relationship because her reputation threatens his family’s honor and his daughter’s marriage prospects. Though heartbroken, Violetta agrees to sacrifice her own happiness. She returns to Paris and pretends to have abandoned Alfredo for another man, causing him to publicly humiliate her at a party.

In the final act, Violetta is gravely ill and nearly abandoned. Alfredo learns the truth about her sacrifice and rushes back to beg forgiveness, followed by his remorseful father. For a brief moment, Violetta dreams of a future with Alfredo, but her strength fails her, and she dies in his arms, transformed from a figure of scandal into one of deep love and self-sacrifice.

An opera by French composer Georges Bizet after the novel of Prosper Mérimée. Carmen, set in Seville, follows Don José, a young soldier whose orderly life unravels after he meets Carmen, a fiercely independent Romani woman who works in a cigarette factory. After Carmen is arrested for fighting, she seduces Don José into helping her escape. Though he is already engaged to the gentle Micaëla, Don José becomes obsessed with Carmen and begins neglecting his duty and former life.

Carmen soon draws Don José into the world of smugglers, but their relationship becomes unstable. Carmen values freedom above all else, while Don José grows increasingly jealous and possessive. Meanwhile, the glamorous bullfighter Escamillo begins courting Carmen, and she becomes attracted to him. Micaëla later finds Don José and begs him to return home to his dying mother, forcing him to leave Carmen for a time.

In the final act, Carmen and Escamillo arrive at the bullring, now openly a couple. Don José confronts Carmen outside the arena and pleads with her to come back to him. Carmen refuses, insisting that she no longer loves him and will not give up her freedom. In a fit of desperation and rage, Don José stabs Carmen to death, breaking over her dead body and demanding for his own arrest.

Most famous for the mysterious Tristan chord, this opera of German composer Richard Wagner is a gigantic achievement in musical storytelling with Leitmotifs.

Tristan und Isolde tells the story of Tristan, a Cornish knight, and Isolde, an Irish princess. Tristan has killed Isolde’s fiancé in battle, but she once healed him when he came to her in disguise. Now Tristan is escorting Isolde by ship to Cornwall, where she is to marry his uncle, King Marke. Furious and humiliated, Isolde plans to drink poison with Tristan, but her maid Brangäne secretly substitutes a love potion. Tristan and Isolde drink it and are overwhelmed by a passionate, forbidden love.

In Cornwall, Isolde becomes King Marke’s bride, but she and Tristan continue to meet in secret at night. Their love is presented as something that cannot exist within the ordinary world of daylight, duty, and social order. Brangäne warns them that they may be discovered, but they ignore her. Eventually, the lovers are betrayed by Melot, one of Tristan’s friends, and King Marke finds them together. Marke is heartbroken, not only because of Isolde’s betrayal but because Tristan, whom he loved and trusted, has deceived him.

Tristan allows himself to be wounded by Melot and is taken back to his ancestral home in Brittany. There, he waits in agony for Isolde to come and heal him again. When her ship finally arrives, Tristan tears off his bandages in excitement and dies in her arms. King Marke then arrives, having learned the truth about the love potion and intending to forgive them, but it is too late. Isolde, overcome by grief and transcendence, sings her final “Liebestod” and dies beside Tristan, imagining their love fulfilled beyond death.

!"The Firebird" is a ballet based on Russian folklore. Prince Ivan wanders into the magical realm of the evil sorcerer Kashchei and captures the glowing Firebird. She begs for freedom, and Ivan releases her; in return, she gives him one of her feathers, promising that he can summon her if he is ever in danger.

Ivan then discovers a group of enchanted princesses, including the beautiful Tsarevna, and falls in love with her. But Kashchei and his monstrous servants appear and threaten him. Ivan uses the feather to call the Firebird, who forces Kashchei’s followers into a wild, exhausting dance and then lulls them to sleep.

The Firebird reveals the secret of Kashchei’s power: his soul is hidden inside a magical egg. Ivan destroys it, breaking the spell over the kingdom. Kashchei dies, his victims are freed, and the enchanted realm is restored. Ivan and the Tsarevna are united in a triumphant ending.

Three small operas, each of them only one act, that together form a whole, similar to a triptychon painting, hence the name.

Il tabarro, “the cloak”, is the tragic act of the three, set on a tugboat on the Seine. After losing her child, Giorgetta, wife of Skipper Michele, begins a secret relationship with harbor worker Luigi, despite swearing love to her husband. After Michele grows suspicious, he discovers Luigi on deck by accident - and subsequently kills him, only to wrap him in the cloak that he used to warm his wife with.

In Gianni Schicchi, the comedic act, the relatives of recently-deceased Buoso Donati gather to hear the reading of his will. Meanwhile, Lauretta is in love with Rinuccio, but he is only allowed to marry a woman of status and money. Gianni Schicchi, her father, pressured by his daughter, comes up with a cunning plan: As the city does not know Donati has died, Gianni Schicchi impersonates him on his deathbed, dictating a new will. The relatives try to bribe him, each for their own benefit, but Schicchi, as Donati’s “best friend” takes most of the inheritance and throws the relatives out, leaving him with the house and a happy couple permitted to marry.

The lyrical work, Sour Angelica, is set in a convent, to which Sister Angelica, daughter to a noble family, was sent to after the birth of an illegitimate child, and only has one wish: For a relative to come visit her. Her wish comes true as her aunt, the Baroness, comes to visit the convent. Having to confess to her that her illegitimate child died two years ago, Angelica is left in deep grief, developing a wish to die herself. After drinking a poisonous potion, she seeks grace in her prayer to Maria, and joins her son in death.

Brazilian composer, cellist and guitarist Heitor Villa Lobos composed this cycle of Etudes during his stay in Paris, and as such, they blend his uniquely Brazilian style with Debussy-like impressionism - with his “Douze Etudes pour piano” being a probable inspiration.

Each of these etudes blends a few techniques of the classical guitar together, and while the technical challenge of them is a milestone for every student, they are also one of the first few big works for the classical guitar, which is only slowly emerging from its niche into a more respectable concert instrument.

Brazilian composer, cellist and guitarist Heitor Villa-Lobos pays tribute to the music of Johann Sebastian Bach, but “brazilianating” his style by combining them with Brazilian folk music, utilizing common elements as a bridge between them, taking Choro-style melodies and combining them with forms of Bach's time. The Bachiana Brasileira No.1 is written for Cello-Orchestra, featuring three movements, with each one getting two titles, one characterizing the Brazilian, the other characterizing the baroque aspect.

The final movement is in the baroque fugue form, where a theme appears over and over again, joined by a secondary theme that counteracts the first. These two themes are used by Villa Lobos also in the form of a Conversa, where two instruments fight for the pole position in the ensemble.

These menuets were composed by a phantom - often being referred to as a Rossini of the New World. Peruvian composer Pedro Ximénez Abril Tirado has been lost to time, with only a handful of his compositions having been known at lifetime under different names like Ximénez or Tirado-Abril, with the majority of his works only to be discovered in the future, with 100 Menuets for Solo Guitar being one of his very few published works that have not been lost.

In a reality where Ximenez would not have become poor and destitute through the exile of his greatest mentor and supporter, president Santa Cruz of Peru and Bolivia, his compositions would have been known by his contemporaries as an inherent part to the musical history of the New World. In his distinctly south-american style, Ximénez blends the classical European forms of composition with the folklore of his home country.

His manuscripts for hundreds of pieces became forgotten and are currently resting in suitcases on the attics of descendants, some of them even being used as insulation material, with the rediscovery of his music only being a prophecy for the future, to start in the distant year 2000.

Originally written for solo piano, numerous arrangements exist, one by the composer himself for a full orchestra. In the six movements of this piece, Cuban composer Ernesto Lecuona refers to six Andalusian landscapes, in very similar fashion to the works of Spanish composer Isaac Albeniz that had been released a few decades prior in 1886.

These pieces are an evocation of Spanish flamenco culture, with typically spanish elements like phrygian scales or andalusian cadences being quite ubiquitous. The basic flamenco forms have many local variants, such as the Malagueña being a fandango variant from Malaga - “Malagueña” is also the title of the sixth movement in this work. This particular Malagueña will later go on to become part of American popular culture, with adaptations such as Jimmy Dorsey’s “at the crossroads” and also as an overplayed piece for solo guitar.

“Only one other waltz vies with the “Blue Danube” for the privilege of being played around the world every day, every hour. It is Sobre las Olas” - Mexican Author José Emilio Pacheco will say about this piece. For his most popular piece, Mexican composer Juventino Rosas wrote a Waltz, a form originating in the German-speaking part of the world, with composers like the Strauss family making an entire living off composing them. Sobre las Olas was composed while sitting at the edge of a stream under a tree, originally called “close to the spring”, but as the chords evoked the gentle movement of a boat on the sea, Rosas changed the piece's name
Zequinha de Abreu: Tico-Tico no Fubá

A very short piece commonly played as an Encore by orchestras, "Tico-tico no Fubá" is a distinctly Brazilian piece. It is written in the Choro form, which originated in Brazilian popular music, mixing traditionally western forms like Polka, Waltz and Mazurkas with the rhythms common to the musicians of Rio de Janeiro. Despite the form being named “Choro”, which literally means “lament”, the music sounds more rhythmical and happy.

"Tico-tico no Fubá" - the sparrow in the cornmeal - consists of three parts in a form that is identical to the classic three-part Rondo, with Samba rhythms that are very similar to those you hear constantly in the New World - because the Artistas like to play that one particular Samba song on their Gramophones so loudly and often.

Alfredo Napoleão lives between the New and Old world, frequently traveling between his parents home of Porto and the cultural cities of the new world in the former La Corona colonies - Just like his two brothers, who are also composers, and his older brother Arthur became known as a publisher and for writing a big cycle of 18 studies for piano that are incredibly difficult to play.

Napoleão writes in the key of e-flat minor, a key so deranged that it even features the note “C-flat”. Any sane person would call that a B - you play it on a white key, but written is a C with a flat sign. Setting aside the unusual key signature and mental gymnastics required to read, the concerto is inspired by a multitude of European composers. The piano part is written in stylistic reference to Chopin with a lot of fluent cascades. The long first movement evokes a sense of mystery and drama, while it also features quite a beautiful secondary theme. The second movement is quite short and reminds more of Saint-Saëns and Mendelssohn, with a stark change in character between the Scherzo and Trio section.

All in all, this concerto is rather a European one - written by a half-European composer who migrated to and lived in the New World, making this concerto a relic from the intense cultural link between them, or better, cultural domination of one through the other, when the New World was under firm La Corona colonialist control.

"Odeon" is a piece for Solo piano, in a form called “maxixe”, also known as a Brazilian Tango, which is closely related to the Choro form. One can hear a bit of Fryderyk Chopin in the composition, whose style influenced Nazareth in his earlier years, but Nazareth’s style is more rhythmical.

Odeon is a Tango in a three-part-rondo structure: A-B-A-C-A, named after the Odeon Cinema in the city of Rio de Janeiro, where its composer often performs on a piano in the waiting area, mesmerizing the people waiting for their movie to start, sometimes said to even be missing them just to listen to Nazareth.

Paraguayan composer and guitarist Agustín Barrios Mangoré writes a piece about a religious man passing by the cathedral of Montevideo, hearing the cathedral organist playing music of Johann Sebastian Bach. The characteristic regular rhythms and baroque chord changes of Bach's music build the foundation for the piece's style.

In a slow, religious Andante, Barrios builds a calm and contemplative atmosphere that reminisces the church, while the third movement, Allegro solemne is a more literal allusion to Johann Sebastian Bach, written in a style similar to Bach’s Allegro movements, but in form of a Rondo.
Julian Aguirre: 5 Tristes from "Aires nacionales argentinos"

Argentinian composer Julian Aguirre writes a piano cycle consisting of 5 tristes, joined by 5 canciones in a second cycle. The triste itself is a distinctly argentinian form of folk music from times when La Corona was not yet colonizing the new World, which developed out of indigenous Incan and Peruvian music, getting named after the melancholy it holds - a melancholy that links directly to the character of the transfigured folk symbol of the gaucho. The style rose to prominence, then fell out of fashion, only to be rediscovered in circuses and by folk singers. Julian Aguirre rather incorporates elements of the triste into his pieces, they are not limited to stylization.

A few characteristics are found in a triste. Melodies often start on the highest note and repeat that, and they nearly always close with a descending motion, with the second-to-last note being very long, which sounds like a sighing gesture. There are a few triste styles of cadence that Aguirre frequently uses in these pieces, like a cadence that approaches the final note first from below, then from above, and triste no. 5 features a very common triste rhythm in the accompaniment outright.

Throughout all tristes, Aguirre makes use of the rhythmic freedom and parlando singing style, and the rhythmic structure is similar to those that are used in a triste usually - although Aguirre doesn’t write the complete triste structures that consist of a tema in 2/4 and a faster kimba in 6/8.
Alberto Williams: La bruja de las montañas

The second symphony of Argentinian composer Alberto Williams bears the title “The witch of the mountains”, sharing this name with a ballad Williams had written earlier. The first movement called “rumors from the mountain”, after a brief exposition, introduces two themes: A dramatic theme that seems to speak of the hidden dangers in the mountains, and a more lyrical one, building towards the program in the subsequent movements, later being contextualized into an evil and a good theme.

In the second movement, called “Prayers of the Monks” the introduction consists of bells, which, in a very literal sense allude to the call to prayer from a church, which is followed by a grave and meditative section.

The third movement “The white pigeons of prayer” briefly introduces a more lively theme, similar in form and character to a scherzo, which is the standard third movement in most symphonies. But this happy character regresses to the same gravity of the second movement, also reintroducing the bells from earlier.

In the final movement, the witch of the mountains shows herself in the form of dramatic percussion, which results in a religious struggle between the heavenly side of prayer and good, characterized through the bells and the lyrical theme, and the hellish side of the witch, represented by a rhythmical theme, with the forces of good ultimately winning, closing the symphony with its lyrical theme.

"Il Guarany" is set in colonial Brazil and centers on the Portuguese nobleman Don Antonio de Mariz, his daughter Cecilia, and the Indigenous Guarani hero Peri. Cecilia is loved by several men, but Peri’s devotion to her is the purest and most selfless. He repeatedly protects her and her family from danger, even though the colonial society around her treats him as an outsider.

The conflict intensifies when Gonzales, a treacherous adventurer, plots against Don Antonio’s household and tries to seize Cecilia. At the same time, the Aimoré people attack in revenge after one of their women has been killed. Peri risks his life for Cecilia, even preparing to sacrifice himself among the Aimoré in order to save her.

In the end, Don Antonio’s home is destroyed, and Peri escapes with Cecilia as catastrophe overwhelms the others. Depending on the version, the ending emphasizes either their survival together or a more symbolic, mythic union between them. The opera closes with Peri and Cecilia carried away from the ruined world of colonial violence, suggesting both romantic devotion and the birth of a new Brazilian legend.
